claim: A novel column-based cultivation method was developed that allowed generation of large numbers of advanced-age yeast cells in a constant environment.
source: Here, we developed a novel column-based cultivation method that allowed us to generate large numbers of advanced-age cells in a constant environment.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and validation of the column-based cultivation method in the Results section and Materials and methods.

claim: The column-based cultivation method maintained constant oxygen, glucose, and pH levels during cultivation.
source: The flowing medium also provided fresh nutrients and oxygen and ensured constant culture conditions, as confirmed for pH, glucose, and oxygen levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C shows measurements confirming constant oxygen, glucose, and pH levels.

claim: Up to 10^9 mother cells could be retained per column.
source: Because we could retain up to 109 mother cells per column (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), we could produce sufficient numbers of aged cells for performing parallel proteome and transcriptome analyses.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 3 shows cell counts present in each sample harvested from the columns.

claim: The viability of mother cells over time in the column-based cultivation method was in excellent agreement with the lifespan curve of yeast observed in a microfluidic device.
source: From this data, we derived the viability of the mother cells over time, which we found to be in excellent agreement with the lifespan curve of yeast as observed in a microfluidic device (Huberts et al., 2014) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows comparison of viability curves from the column method and microfluidic device data from Huberts et al., 2014.

claim: Aging yeast cells show increased cell size.
source: Using the forward scatter of the flow cytometer as a rough proxy for cell size, we could qualitatively observe the cell size increase of live mothers that is known to occur in aging mother cells (Egilmez et al., 1990) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Figure 1C shows forward scatter data indicating cell size increase with age, and citation to Egilmez et al., 1990 provides literature support.

claim: Aging yeast cells accumulate bud scars.
source: Similarly, using fluorophore-conjugated wheat-germ agglutinin, which labels bud scars that appear after every division (Powell et al., 2003), we observed an increase of bud scar staining on mother cells in the column, as also visualized by confocal microscopy (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D show bud scar staining and counting data, with citation to Powell et al., 2003.

claim: A mathematical un-mixing method was developed to determine the molecular phenotype of aging mother cells without contributions from daughter or dead cells.
source: Next, we developed a combined experimental and mathematical method to determine the molecular phenotype of aging mother cells without contributions from daughter or dead cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes the mathematical un-mixing approach and its validation in the Results section and supplemental notes.

claim: The mathematical un-mixing method was validated with <16% average error for RNAseq transcriptome, targeted proteome, and global proteome data.
source: Experiments using samples containing mixed cell populations with known molecular phenotypes validated this mathematical un-mixing method for the RNA sequencing (RNAseq) transcriptome, targeted (selected reaction monitoring) proteome, and global (shotgun) proteome data with a <16% average error (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2 show validation results for the un-mixing method.

claim: The final datasets consisted of profiles for 1494 proteins and 4904 transcripts from aging mother cells.
source: This yielded profiles for 1494 proteins and 4904 transcripts from aging mother cells.
evidence: The manuscript states the number of proteins and transcripts in the final dataset.

claim: Proteomes of aging mother cells diverge from the youthful state over time.
source: Correlation analyses between the proteomes of young cells and the proteomes of aging mother cells confirmed the expected divergence of the aging cell away from the youthful state (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3A shows Spearman correlation decreasing over time between young and aging mother cell proteomes.

claim: Daughters from later time points showed a partially aged signature.
source: Daughters from later time points showed a partially aged signature (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with the notion that rejuvenation of daughter cells is incomplete later in a mother's life (Kennedy et al., 1994).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows daughter cell profiles with aging signatures, and citation to Kennedy et al., 1994 provides literature support.

claim: Specific proteome changes detected in the study agree with observations in literature, including changes related to glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, energy reserve pathways, stress response proteins, and mitochondrial changes.
source: Furthermore, we found agreement between specific proteome changes detected by us and observations present in literature, including changes related to glycolysis, gluconeogenesis (Lin et al., 2001), increased expression levels in energy reserve pathway proteins (Levy et al., 2012), increases in stress response protein levels (Erjavec et al., 2007; Crane et al., 2014), and mitochondrial changes (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 show proteome changes, with multiple citations to literature.

claim: Levels of the stress-related chaperone Hsp104 and the translation elongation factor Tef1 increase with age at the single-cell level.
source: Specifically, we see the levels of the stress-related chaperone Hsp104 and the translation elongation factor Tef1 to increase with age (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), similar to what was shown using a microfluidic platform tracking single cells (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 4 shows single-cell level protein dynamics, with citation to Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: 64% of proteins that showed a twofold change by the end of the yeast lifespan also showed a significant change in the same direction at an earlier time point.
source: Specifically, we found that 64% (184/288 total changes) of the proteins that showed a twofold change by the end of the yeast lifespan also showed a significant change in the same direction at an earlier time point (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative analysis of protein changes over time shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Aging is a gradual process occurring from early on.
source: These findings suggest that aging is a gradual process occurring from early on.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that changes start at young age and are gradual and mostly unidirectional.

claim: The correlation between proteome and transcriptome declined steadily with age, from 0.75 to 0.70.
source: When comparing this correlation in time, however, we found that it declined steadily with age, down to a correlation of 0.70 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Figure 5A shows the declining Spearman correlation between proteome and transcriptome over time.

claim: Protein levels become increasingly uncoupled from their transcript levels during aging.
source: These results indicate that, over time, protein levels were increasingly uncoupled from their transcript levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreasing correlation between proteome and transcriptome and different GO terms describing changes in proteins vs transcripts.

claim: 38.4% of analyzed transcript-protein pairs were located in quadrant 2 of the co-expression map, where proteins were over-represented relative to their transcripts.
source: Of all analyzed transcript–protein pairs, 38.4% were located in Q2, suggesting a global tendency towards relative protein overabundance with aging (Figure 5).
evidence: Figure 5B shows the co-expression map with genes distributed across quadrants.

claim: Quadrant 2 of the co-expression map was strongly enriched in 'translation regulation' gene products (i.e. ribosome and protein biogenesis machinery).
source: Strikingly, Q2 was strongly enriched in 'translation regulation' gene products (i.e. ribosome and protein biogenesis machinery) (Figure 5B), and the extent of their overabundance progressively increased as the cells aged (Figure 5—figure supplement 2,3).
evidence: Figure 5B shows GO term enrichments for quadrant 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2,3 show the progressive increase in overabundance.

claim: A high-level directional network was reconstructed to reveal the interdependences of changes in transcript expression during aging.
source: To elucidate the causal order of changes during aging, we reconstructed a high-level directional network revealing the interdependences of changes in transcript expression (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 6 shows the high-level directional network, and the manuscript describes the network reconstruction method.

claim: The very first causal-ranked cluster in the transcriptome network was highly enriched for gene products associated with protein biogenesis (i.e. ribosome biogenesis and tRNA processing).
source: This high-level directional network of the transcriptome data showed that the very first causal-ranked cluster in the network that we detected was highly enriched for gene products associated with protein biogenesis (i.e. ribosome biogenesis and transfer RNA [tRNA] processing; Figure 6B).
evidence: Figure 6B shows the causal ranking of clusters with GO term enrichments.

claim: Genes from the most causal cluster in the transcriptome network were enriched in quadrant 2 of the co-expression map, which showed uncoupled expression.
source: These are the same biological processes that had uncoupled transcript and protein levels (Figure 5B); indeed, genes from this causal cluster were enriched in Q2 of the co-expression map, which showed uncoupled expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B show the enrichment of cluster 1 genes in quadrant 2.

claim: The uncoupling of protein and transcript levels for 'biogenesis'-related genes has a central role in the aging process and may affect the transcript and protein abundances of other genes.
source: These analyses suggest that the uncoupling of protein and transcript levels for 'biogenesis'-related genes has a central role in the aging process, and may affect the transcript and protein abundances of other genes, as elaborated upon in the discussion.
evidence: This is inferred from the network analysis showing biogenesis genes as most causal and their uncoupled expression.

claim: An increased deviation from the original stoichiometry of protein complexes occurred with aging.
source: Indeed, using curated lists of protein complexes (Cherry et al., 2012), we found that an increased deviation from the original stoichiometry occurred with aging (Figure 7B–D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1–3).
evidence: Figure 7B-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1-3 show loss of stoichiometry in protein complexes over time.

claim: The vacuolar adenosine triphosphatase and the nuclear pore complex lose stoichiometry with aging.
source: We observed many complexes that were not previously implicated in aging to be age-affected, and we found previously implicated protein complexes such as the vacuolar adenosine triphosphatase (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012) and the nuclear pore complex (Lord et al., 2015; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014) to lose stoichiometry (Figure 7C and D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1,2).
evidence: Figure 7C and D show loss of stoichiometry in these complexes, with citations to literature.

claim: The global stoichiometry loss was greater in aged mothers compared with the daughter population.
source: The global stoichiometry loss was greater in aged mothers compared with the daughter population (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A), confirming that this is an aging-related phenotype.
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 3A shows comparison of stoichiometry loss between mothers and daughters.

claim: The stoichiometry loss was greater overall at the proteome level than at the transcriptome level.
source: Additionally, we found that the stoichiometry loss was greater overall at the proteome level than at the transcriptome level (Figure 7B), supporting the observation that protein levels uncouple from their transcript levels.
evidence: Figure 7B shows bean plots comparing stoichiometry loss in proteome vs transcriptome.

claim: The uncoupling of protein levels of biogenesis-related genes from their transcript levels is causal for the changes occurring in aging yeast.
source: Based on these analyses, we propose a model whereby the uncoupling of protein levels of biogenesis-related genes from their transcript levels is causal for the changes occurring in aging yeast.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the integration of multiple analyses including co-expression maps and network inference.

claim: Proteins of the translation machinery that are uncoupled from transcript levels accumulate in cells with age.
source: The model proposes that proteins of the translation machinery that are uncoupled from transcript levels accumulate in cells with age (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows translation regulation genes in quadrant 2 with protein overabundance relative to transcripts.

claim: The uncoupling of biogenesis genes might contribute to further uncoupling of the proteome from the transcriptome as a whole.
source: As the biogenesis genes are themselves involved in translation, their uncoupling might contribute to further uncoupling of the proteome from the transcriptome as a whole.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the role of biogenesis genes in translation.

claim: General uncoupling of the proteome from the transcriptome has degenerative effects including cell size increase, protein aggregations, and loss of stoichiometry in protein complexes.
source: This general uncoupling has degenerative effects (i.e. cell size increase, protein aggregations and loss of stoichiometry in protein complexes), that stimulate transcriptional responses in the cell (i.e. metabolic changes and activated stress responses), which further contributes to changes in the proteome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed consequences of uncoupling described in the Results section.

claim: Ribosomal proteins are highly translated and highly stable.
source: Ribosome footprinting has shown these proteins to be highly translated (Ingolia et al., 2009), and protein turnover experiments have shown them to be highly stable (Belle et al., 2006); thus, it is possible that their overabundance may result from the combination of the dynamics of protein biogenesis, protein turnover, and mRNA stability.
evidence: Citations to Ingolia et al., 2009 and Belle et al., 2006 provide literature support for these properties.

claim: Ribosomal proteins showed a low degree of loss of stoichiometry at the protein complex level.
source: Interestingly, the ribosomal proteins themselves showed a low degree of loss of stoichiometry at the protein complex level in our data (Figure 7C), supporting the idea that they are still active and contributing to uncoupling in the cell.
evidence: Figure 7C shows ribosome complex stoichiometry over time.

claim: Cell size may increase due to protein overproduction and result in metabolic changes.
source: First, cell size may increase due to protein overproduction and result in metabolic changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed protein overproduction and known relationship between cell size and metabolism.

claim: Proteins being overproduced at different rates will alter protein complex stoichiometry.
source: Second, proteins being overproduced at different rates will alter protein complex stoichiometry.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observed uncoupling and loss of stoichiometry.

claim: Many documented phenotypes of aging may result from altered protein complex stoichiometry, including the formation of protein aggregates, increased reactive oxygen species formation by a dysfunctional mitochondrial transport chain, and loss of gene silencing.
source: Many documented phenotypes of aging may result from this, including the formation of protein aggregates (Erjavec et al., 2007), increased reactive oxygen species formation by a dysfunctional mitochondrial transport chain (Laun et al., 2001), and loss of gene silencing (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: Citations to Erjavec et al., 2007, Laun et al., 2001, and Hu et al., 2014 provide literature support for these phenotypes.

claim: Altering the rates of protein production (i.e. translation) or degradation (i.e. autophagy) have repeatedly been shown to influence longevity across a wide range of organisms.
source: Indeed, altering the rates of protein production (i.e. translation) or degradation (i.e. autophagy) have repeatedly been shown to influence longevity across a wide range of organisms (see (Wasko and Kaeberlein, 2014; Johnson et al., 2013; Cuervo, 2008).
evidence: Citations to Wasko and Kaeberlein, 2014, Johnson et al., 2013, and Cuervo, 2008 provide literature support.

claim: Decreases in activity of translation activators TOR and S6 kinase result in increased lifespan in yeast, worms, flies, and mice.
source: The translation activators, target of rapamycin (TOR) and S6 kinase, fall into this category, and decreases in their activity result in increased lifespan in yeast (Fabrizio et al., 2001; Kaeberlein et al., 2005), worms (Vellai et al., 2003; Pan et al., 2007), flies (Kapahi et al., 2004), and mice (Lamming et al., 2012; Selman et al., 2009), as does calorie restriction and drugs such as rapamycin, which are also modulators of protein biogenesis pathways (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: Multiple citations provide literature support for lifespan extension effects across organisms.

claim: Deletions in ribosomal subunit components have positive effects on lifespan in both yeast and worms.
source: Likewise, deletions in ribosomal subunit components have positive effects on lifespan in both yeast (Steffen et al., 2008) and worms (Hansen et al., 2007).
evidence: Citations to Steffen et al., 2008 and Hansen et al., 2007 provide literature support.

claim: The model explains why interventions targeting protein synthesis, or repairing the downstream consequences, can serve as interventions in aging.
source: Our model explains why targeting protein synthesis, or repairing the downstream consequences, can serve as interventions in aging.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract and elaborated in the Discussion based on the proposed model.

claim: Aging is a main risk factor for cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer.
source: Aging, the gradual decrease in function occurring at the molecular, cellular, and organismal level, is a main risk factor for cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer (Niccoli and Partridge, 2012).
evidence: Citation to Niccoli and Partridge, 2012 provides literature support.

claim: The rate of aging is influenced by diverse factors, including protein translation, protein quality control, mitochondrial dysfunction, and metabolism.
source: The rate of aging, however, is influenced by diverse factors, including protein translation, protein quality control, mitochondrial dysfunction, and metabolism (Kennedy and Kaeberlein, 2009; Webb and Brunet, 2014; Lagouge and Larsson, 2013; Barzilai et al., 2012).
evidence: Multiple citations provide literature support for these factors.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae can produce 20–30 daughter cells before its death.
source: Important insights into the complex process of aging originate from research on the unicellular eukaryote Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which can produce 20–30 daughter cells before its death (Mortimer and Johnston, 1959, and see Wasko and Kaeberlein, 2014; Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014 for recent reviews).
evidence: Citation to Mortimer and Johnston, 1959 provides original observation, with additional review citations.

claim: The prototrophic Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain YSBN6 (MATa) was used for the phenotyping of yeast replicative aging.
source: The prototrophic Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain YSBN6 (MATa) was used for the phenotyping of yeast replicative aging (Canelas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with citation to Canelas et al., 2010.

claim: Cells were grown in yeast nitrogen base (YNB) without amino acids supplemented with 2% glucose at 30°C.
source: The cells were grown in yeast nitrogen base (YNB) without amino acids (ForMedium, Norfolk, UK) supplemented with 2% glucose at a temperature of 30°C, unless indicated differently.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Biotinylated cells were labeled with streptavidin-coated iron beads.
source: To obtain aged yeast cells, we bound streptavidin-conjugated iron beads to biotinylated cells (adapted from Smeal et al., 1996) from an exponentially growing culture.
evidence: This is described in the Results section with citation to Smeal et al., 1996.

claim: Daughter cells do not inherit the iron beads because the yeast cell wall remains with the mother during mitosis.
source: The daughter cells do not inherit the iron beads, as the yeast cell wall remains with the mother during mitosis (Smeal et al., 1996).
evidence: Citation to Smeal et al., 1996 provides support for this mechanism.

claim: The age distribution of cells broadened over time in the column cultivation.
source: Computer simulations showed that the age distribution broadened over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B shows simulated age distributions at different time points.

claim: Cells were harvested at exponentially increasing time intervals to maximize the differences between time points at later ages.
source: The broadened age distribution results in a lower resolution making detecting the actual changes occurring at later time points more difficult, and we therefore harvested cells at exponentially increasing time intervals to maximize the differences between time points at later ages.
evidence: This is explained in the Results section based on the modeling of age distributions.

claim: Two replicate campaigns were performed, generating 16 unique time points in total.
source: Finally, we performed two replicate runs of the column-captured cell culturing campaigns. Campaign 1 generated an unprocessed sample and 14 column samples and campaign 2 generated another unprocessed sample and 8 column samples. In total, two unprocessed samples combined with 16 unique time points were generated (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 5 shows the experimental pipeline with replicate campaigns.

claim: The replicates of proteome and transcriptome data were in excellent agreement with Spearman correlations >0.85.
source: We found the replicates to be in excellent agreement (Spearman correlations >0.85) (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Figure 2B,C shows correlation plots between replicates.

claim: A coefficient of variation cutoff of 0.3 was used to select the most reproducible expression profiles, consisting of ~90.9% of the proteome and ~84.4% of the transcriptome datasets.
source: The coefficient of variation was calculated between the replicate datasets for each gene-product profile and a cutoff of 0.3 was used to select the most reproducible expression profiles between replicates, consisting of ∼90.9% of the proteome, and ∼84.4% of the transcriptome datasets.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The starting correlation between proteome and transcriptome was 0.75, in agreement with other single-study comparisons between yeast proteomes and transcriptomes.
source: To compare the changes between the proteome and transcriptome, we determined the non-parametric Spearman rank correlation, and found a starting correlation of 0.75, a value in agreement with other single-study comparisons between yeast proteomes and transcriptomes (Csárdi et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to Csárdi et al., 2015 provides comparison to literature values.

claim: The decreasing trend in proteome-transcriptome correlation is not an experimental artefact.
source: Furthermore, this trend is also not an experimental artefact, since samples originating from all time points were treated identically, and both proteome and transcriptome datasets originated from the same biological samples.
evidence: This is stated as a control consideration in the Results section.

claim: At increased cell size and low rates of glucose influx, cells switch to respiration.
source: Increased cell size could reduce glucose influx rates per cell volume and induce metabolic changes, for example, at low rates of glucose influx, cells switch to respiration (Huberts et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to Huberts et al., 2012 provides support for this metabolic relationship.

claim: Metabolic signatures related to starvation and oxidative stress were consequences of aging found in the transcript-based network analysis and proteome dataset.
source: Indeed, in our transcript-based network analysis (Figure 6B) as well as in our proteome dataset (Figure 3B), we found that metabolic signatures related to starvation and oxidative stress were consequences of aging.
evidence: Figure 6B and Figure 3B show these metabolic signatures.

claim: The most causal cluster of the proteome network was enriched for chaperone proteins.
source: The most causal cluster of the proteome network was enriched for chaperone proteins, reflecting a cellular response to internally changing conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the proteome network analysis.

claim: The causal clusters of the proteome network tended to be expressed according to their transcriptional message (i.e. coupled expression), while the responsive clusters represented increasingly uncoupled expression.
source: Furthermore, we found that the causal clusters of the proteome network tended to be expressed according to their transcriptional message (i.e. coupled expression; Q1, Q3), while the responsive clusters represented increasingly uncoupled expression (Q2, Q4) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 2C shows enrichment analysis of network clusters in co-expression quadrants.
